extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, evolution equations, variational formulae, and monotonicity results used to define Perelman's reduced distance and reduced volume for Ricci flow, and the application to no-local-collapsing. Focused on analytic and geometric arguments (L-length, L-geodesics, Jacobian comparison, monotonicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of H (Li-Yau type integrand)
rubrics_metrics.description: H = 2Δf − |∇f|^2 + R + (f − n)/τ (equivalently rewritten as (2.6.8) H = 2 ∂f/∂τ + ... + 1/τ f in the text). H is the Li–Yau type quantity associated to a solution f of the conjugate heat equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H appears as the integrand for Perelman's W-functional and is used to derive Li–Yau type estimates for fundamental solutions of the conjugate heat equation. See equation (2.6.8) and the surrounding derivation; the exact form is used to compute evolution and apply the maximum principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution equations for H and v
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the backward Ricci flow (τ = T − t), H and v = τ H u satisfy explicit evolution equations of the form ∂H/∂τ = ΔH − 2∇f·∇H − (1/τ)H − 2τ|∇∇f − (1/2τ)g|^2 − ... and ∂v/∂τ = Δv − Rv + ... (text gives the exact expanded formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These evolution formulae are derived by direct computation and are central to applying the parabolic maximum principle to quantities involving H and to derive monotonicity properties. Use them when analyzing behavior of fundamental solutions or the W-functional integrand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principle consequence: monotonicity of τH
rubrics_metrics.description: By the maximum principle, max(τ H) is nonincreasing as τ increases; in particular for fundamental solutions one can show lim_{τ→0} τ H ≤ 0 (and H ≤ 0 once normalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Li–Yau-type estimate (Perelman's estimate) is used to control terms in the Li–Yau path integral and to derive heat-kernel-type bounds for solutions of the conjugate heat equation. The text omits detailed proof for the fundamental-solution limit but indicates the consequence is standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of L-length (Lτ(γ))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth space curve γ(τ), 0 < τ1 ≤ τ2, the L-length is defined L_{τ1}^{τ2}(γ) = ∫_{τ1}^{τ2} √τ ( R(γ(τ),τ) + |γ̇(τ)|_{g(τ)}^2 ) dτ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functional (the Li–Yau / Perelman L-length) is the quantity to be minimized to define reduced distance; it plays the role of a 'space-time length' and is the integrand appearing after applying the Li–Yau estimate. It is used to define L-geodesics and the reduced distance L(q,τ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Li–Yau–Perelman distance (reduced distance) l(q,τ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given fixed base point p at τ=0, the L-distance L(q,τ) is the minimal L-length over curves joining p to q (with τ1=0). The reduced distance is l(q,τ) = L(q,τ)/(2√τ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reduced distance provides a space-time distance used to weight points in Perelman's reduced volume. It is the key quantity in relating heat-kernel estimates to geometric monotonicity; see (2.6.9)-(2.6.10) and subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: First variation formula for L-length (Lemma 3.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The variation δ_Y(L) equals boundary term 2√τ ⟨X,Y⟩|_{τ1}^{τ2} plus integral terms: ∫_{τ1}^{τ2} √τ ⟨Y, ∇R − 2∇_X X − (1/τ)X + 4Ric(X,·)⟩ dτ (as stated in Lemma 3.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this first variation formula to characterize critical curves (L-geodesics) and to compute gradients of L(q,τ) with respect to spatial variations. The lemma yields formulas (3.2.2) and (3.2.3) for ∇L and ∂_τ L.

rubrics_metrics.name: L-geodesic (Euler–Lagrange equation for L)
rubrics_metrics.description: A smooth curve γ(τ) is an L-geodesic if it satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation (3.2.1): ∇_X X − (1/2)∇R + (1/2τ)X + 2 Ric(X,·) = 0 (with X = γ̇).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence: for any two points p,q and τ2>τ1>0 there exists a minimizing L-geodesic; one can extend definition to τ1=0 by taking limit of √τ γ̇. L-geodesics are the curves used to define L-distance and reduced distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second variation formula for L-length (Lemma 3.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second variation δ^2_Y(L) is expressed as boundary term plus ∫ √τ [2|∇_X Y|^2 + 2⟨R(Y,X)Y,X⟩ + ∇_Y∇_Y R + 2∇_X Ric(Y,Y) − 4∇_Y Ric(Y,X)] dτ (as given in Lemma 3.2.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This index form is used to estimate Hessians of L and to obtain comparison inequalities; equality characterizes Jacobi fields/variations by L-geodesics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hessian and Laplacian estimates for L (Corollary 3.2.4 / Prop 3.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a unit vector Y extended along an L-shortest geodesic via ODE (3.2.8), Hess L(Y,Y) ≤ (1/√τ) − 2√τ Ric(Y,Y) − ∫_0^{τ} √s Q(X,Y) ds, and summing over an orthonormal frame yields ∆L ≤ (n/√τ) − 2√τ R − (1/τ)K where K = ∫_0^{τ} s^{3/2} Q(X) ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inequalities relate second derivatives of L (and hence of l) to curvature and the Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic Q; they are central to deriving the PDE inequalities for l used in monotonicity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential inequalities for reduced distance l (Lemma 3.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduced distance l(q,τ) satisfies distributional inequalities: ∂_τ l = −l/τ + R + (1/2τ^{3/2})K; |∇l|^2 = −R + l/τ − (1/τ^{3/2})K/2; and ∆l ≤ −R + l/τ − (1/2τ^{3/2})K (see (3.2.11)-(3.2.13)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations enable the key inequality ∂_τ − ∆ + R applied to (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l} is nonnegative, which underlies monotonicity of the reduced volume. Equality cases characterize gradient shrinking solitons.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDE inequality for the reduced volume density
rubrics_metrics.description: The combination yields ∂_τ − ∆ + R applied to (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l} is ≥ 0; equivalently (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l} evolves subharmonically with a favourable sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrating this inequality (and using either compactness or decay conditions) gives monotonicity of the integral ˜V(τ). This is the analytic core of Perelman's monotonicity argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Perelman's reduced volume ˜V(τ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For compact M (or under suitable completeness/bounded-curvature hypotheses), define ˜V(τ) = (4πτ)^{-n/2} ∫_M e^{-l(q,τ)} dV_τ(q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: analog of heat-kernel mass; used as a monotone quantity under Ricci flow. The integrand is the reduced volume density (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and finiteness of reduced volume (Theorem 3.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If gij(τ) is a complete solution to backward Ricci flow ∂_τ g = 2Ric with bounded curvature (or M compact), then (i) ˜V(τ) is finite and nonincreasing in τ, and (ii) the monotonicity is strict unless the solution is a gradient shrinking soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Jacobian comparison along L-geodesics, short-time asymptotics of L and J(τ) as τ→0, and the PDE inequality for the density. Finiteness follows from Gaussian asymptotics l(0)=|v|^2/2 and J→1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem (Theorem 3.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Along any shortest L-geodesic γ starting from p, the quantity (4πτ)^{-n/2} e^{-l(τ)} J(τ) is nonincreasing in τ (where J is the L-Jacobian of the L-exponential map).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the geodesic-level comparison principle that integrates to give monotonicity of ˜V(τ). It combines the Hessian/Laplacian bounds for L with the evolution of Jacobian determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-time asymptotics for L and Jacobian
rubrics_metrics.description: As τ→0 along an L-geodesic with limit √τ γ̇ → v, one has l(0) = |v|^2/2 and J(τ) → 1; moreover, estimates show controlled behaviour for small τ (see (3.2.18)-(3.2.19)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These asymptotics are used to show integrability of the reduced volume density near τ=0 and to identify the initial Gaussian weight that bounds the integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of extended manifold ˜M and identification of Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic (Proposition 3.1.1 & Corollary 3.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider ˜M = M × S^N × R^+ with metric ˜g whose components are chosen so that as N→∞ (modulo O(1/N)) curvature components of ˜g coincide with the Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic; in particular ˜Ric = 0 modulo O(1/N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric construction explains the origin of the Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic as a curvature operator on a higher-dimensional space and motivates the reduced-volume monotonicity via (formal) Bishop-Gromov volume comparison applied to ˜g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li–Yau–Hamilton quadratic Q and its decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Q = M_{ij} W_i W_j + 2 P_{ijk} U_{ij} W_k + R_{ijkl} U_{ij} U_{kl}, with M_{ij} = ΔR_{ij} − ... and P_{ijk} = ∇_i R_{jk} − ∇_j R_{ik} (definitions given in text). Q appears in second-variation/index-form expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Q enters the integral terms K and the curvature-correcting terms in evolution/Hessian bounds. Control of Q (signs/estimates) is used in comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No local collapsing: definition of κ-noncollapsed at scale r (Def 3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution g_{ij}(t) is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on scale r if whenever |Rm|(x,t) ≤ r^{-2} for all x in B_{t0}(x0,r) and t ∈ [t0−r^2, t0], then Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the notion of local noncollapsing used by Perelman: control of curvature on a parabolic neighborhood implies a lower volume bound of the corresponding spatial ball at the final time. The constants κ and scale r are uniform quantifiers in theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: No local collapsing theorem I (Theorem 3.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any initial metric on a compact n-manifold M, the Ricci flow solution g_{ij}(t) on [0,T) has constants κ>0 and ρ0>0 such that for any t0∈[0,T) and any x0∈M the solution is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on all scales less than ρ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses monotonicity of reduced volume and a contradiction argument: if collapsing occurs on smaller and smaller scales, one derives a contradiction with reduced volume lower bounds. This theorem provides local injectivity-radius/volume control from curvature bounds and is robust under surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of equality (gradient shrinking soliton condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality in the monotonicity (for l inequalities / reduced volume) holds if and only if the manifold is a gradient shrinking soliton satisfying Rij + (1/2√τ) ∇_i ∇_j L = (1/2τ) g_{ij} (as stated in Corollary/Proposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies the rigidity case: monotonicity is strict unless the solution is exactly a gradient shrinking soliton, which serves as the equality model in the comparison formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses on the Ricci flow for the arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout: use backward Ricci flow ∂_τ g_{ij} = 2R_{ij} (equivalently τ = T−t). Assumptions: either M compact or metrics g_{ij}(τ) are complete and have uniformly bounded curvature; these guarantee existence of minimizing L-geodesics and applicability of Shi estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical hypotheses are required for the derivations (existence/regularity of L-geodesics, Jacobian estimates, integrability of reduced volume). In noncompact cases bounded curvature and completeness are repeatedly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between v and Perelman's W-functional
rubrics_metrics.description: v = τ H u (with u the conjugate-heat solution) is the integrand of Perelman's W-functional: W(g,f,τ) = ∫ v dV and dW/dτ equals an integral of a nonpositive quantity (hence W is monotone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links the pointwise Li–Yau quantity H and the global W-functional monotonicity; the same evolution computations that show monotonicity of τH feed into monotonicity of W when integrating.
